title: 03. Data Prep & Feature Engineering: Handling Missing Values
summary: The Problem: Real-world data is messy - sensors fail, users skip forms, data gets corrupted
objectives: Why Do We Have Missing Values?

sections.title: Overview
sections.body:
**The Problem:** Real-world data is messy - sensors fail, users skip forms, data gets corrupted

**Why This Matters:** Most ML algorithms crash on missing values. But HOW you handle them dramatically affects model performance. Delete too much → lose information. Impute poorly → introduce bias.

sections.title: Why Do We Have Missing Values?
sections.body:
### **Understanding the "Why" Helps You Choose the Right Strategy**

**1. Missing Completely at Random (MCAR)**
- **Why:** Pure randomness (sensor glitch, coin flip)
- **Example:** Weather sensor randomly fails 5% of the time
- **Safe to:** Delete or impute - no bias introduced

**2. Missing at Random (MAR)**
- **Why:** Missing depends on OTHER observed variables
- **Example:** Older people more likely to skip "income" question
- **Safe to:** Impute using other features (age predicts income)

**3. Missing Not at Random (MNAR)**
- **Why:** Missing depends on the value itself!
- **Example:** High earners skip income question (privacy)
- **Dangerous:** Simple imputation introduces bias!

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Demonstrate missing patterns
np.random.seed(42)

# MCAR: Completely random
data_mcar = pd.DataFrame({
    'age': np.random.randint(20, 70, 100),
    'income': np.random.randint(20000, 100000, 100)
})
# Randomly delete 20% income values
mcar_mask = np.random.rand(100) > 0.8
data_mcar.loc[mcar_mask, 'income'] = np.nan

print("Missing Completely at Random (MCAR):")
print(f"  Missing values: {data_mcar['income'].isna().sum()}")
print(f"  Mean age (with income): {data_mcar[~data_mcar['income'].isna()]['age'].mean():.1f}")
print(f"  Mean age (without income): {data_mcar[data_mcar['income'].isna()]['age'].mean():.1f}")
print("  → No difference! Missing is random ✅")

# MAR: Depends on age
data_mar = pd.DataFrame({
    'age': np.random.randint(20, 70, 100),
    'income': np.random.randint(20000, 100000, 100)
})
# Older people more likely to have missing income
mar_mask = (data_mar['age'] > 50) & (np.random.rand(100) > 0.5)
data_mar.loc[mar_mask, 'income'] = np.nan

print("\n\nMissing at Random (MAR):")
print(f"  Missing values: {data_mar['income'].isna().sum()}")
print(f"  Mean age (with income): {data_mar[~data_mar['income'].isna()]['age'].mean():.1f}")
print(f"  Mean age (without income): {data_mar[data_mar['income'].isna()]['age'].mean():.1f}")
print("  → Older people have more missing! Can use age to impute ✅")

# MNAR: High incomes are missing
data_mnar = pd.DataFrame({
    'age': np.random.randint(20, 70, 100),
    'income': np.random.randint(20000, 100000, 100)
})
# High earners don't report income
mnar_mask = data_mnar['income'] > 70000
data_mnar.loc[mnar_mask, 'income'] = np.nan

print("\n\nMissing Not at Random (MNAR):")
print(f"  Missing values: {data_mnar['income'].isna().sum()}")
print(f"  Mean observed income: ${data_mnar['income'].mean():.0f}")
print(f"  True mean (before deletion): ${np.mean(np.random.randint(20000, 100000, 100)):.0f}")
print("  → Missing high values! Simple imputation creates bias! ⚠️")
```

sections.title: Strategy 1: Deletion
sections.body:
### **When:** MCAR only + plenty of data

**WHY IT WORKS:**
- Removes all bias (you're not making up data)
- Simple, fast
- **No leakage risk**

**WHY IT FAILS:**
- **Loses information** (maybe important patterns)
- Reduces sample size
- Can't delete if missing pattern is informative!

**Code:**
```python
# Example dataset
df = pd.DataFrame({
    'age': [25, 30, np.nan, 45, 50, np.nan, 60],
    'income': [30000, np.nan, 45000, np.nan, 70000, 80000, np.nan],
    'purchased': [0, 1, 1, 0, 1, 1, 0]
})

print("Original data:")
print(df)
print(f"\nRows: {len(df)}")

# Drop rows with ANY missing
df_dropna = df.dropna()
print("\n\nAfter dropna():")
print(df_dropna)
print(f"Rows: {len(df_dropna)} ← Lost {len(df) - len(df_dropna)} rows ({(len(df)-len(df_dropna))/len(df)*100:.0f}%)")

print("\n⚠️  WHY this is dangerous:")
print(f"  Original sample size: {len(df)}")
print(f"  After deletion: {len(df_dropna)}")
print("  → May have deleted important patterns!")

# Better: Drop only if too many missing
threshold = 0.5  # Keep rows with <50% missing
df_threshold = df.dropna(thresh=int(threshold * len(df.columns)))
print(f"\n✅ Better: Keep rows with <{threshold*100:.0f}% missing:")
print(df_threshold)
print(f"Rows: {len(df_threshold)} (kept more data!)")
```

**WHEN TO USE:**
- ✅ MCAR (random missing)
- ✅ Large dataset (>10k samples)
- ✅ <5% missing values
- ❌ Small dataset
- ❌ MAR or MNAR (pattern in missing)

diagrams.title: Handling missing values
diagrams.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  m["Column with missing values"] --> why{"Why is it missing?"}
  why -->|"random, few rows"| drop["Drop rows or impute the median"]
  why -->|"meaningful — no loan → no loan amount"| flag["Impute AND add an is_missing flag"]
  why -->|"related to other features"| adv["KNN or iterative imputation"]
  drop --> fit["Fit the imputer on train only, inside a Pipeline"]
  flag --> fit
  adv --> fit
diagrams.explain: Missingness often carries information, so a simple indicator column can be one of the most useful features. Whatever imputation you choose, it is a learned transformation: fit it on the training folds only, ideally inside a scikit-learn Pipeline so cross-validation stays honest.

sections.title: Strategy 2: Simple Imputation
sections.body:
### **2A. Mean/Median Imputation**

**WHY IT WORKS:**
- Fast, simple
- Preserves sample size
- Median robust to outliers

**WHY IT CAN FAIL:**
- **Reduces variance** (all missing → same value)
- Ignores relationships between features
- Can create "impossible" values

**Code:**
```python
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer

# Generate data with missing values
np.random.seed(42)
ages = np.random.normal(40, 15, 100)
ages[ages < 18] = 18  # Minimum age
ages[np.random.rand(100) < 0.2] = np.nan  # 20% missing

print("Original age distribution:")
print(f"  Mean: {np.nanmean(ages):.1f}")
print(f"  Std:  {np.nanstd(ages):.1f}")
print(f"  Missing: {np.isnan(ages).sum()}")

# Mean imputation
imputer_mean = SimpleImputer(strategy='mean')
ages_mean_imputed = imputer_mean.fit_transform(ages.reshape(-1, 1)).ravel()

print("\n✅ After mean imputation:")
print(f"  Mean: {ages_mean_imputed.mean():.1f} ← Preserved!")
print(f"  Std:  {ages_mean_imputed.std():.1f} ← REDUCED! ⚠️")

# Visualize
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4))

axes[0].hist(ages[~np.isnan(ages)], bins=20, alpha=0.7, edgecolor='black')
axes[0].set_title('Original (without missing)')
axes[0].set_xlabel('Age')
axes[0].set_ylabel('Frequency')
axes[0].axvline(np.nanmean(ages), color='red', linestyle='--', label='Mean')
axes[0].legend()

axes[1].hist(ages_mean_imputed, bins=20, alpha=0.7, edgecolor='black', color='orange')
axes[1].set_title('After Mean Imputation')
axes[1].set_xlabel('Age')
axes[1].axvline(ages_mean_imputed.mean(), color='red', linestyle='--', label='Mean')
axes[1].legend()
axes[1].annotate('Spike at mean!', xy=(ages_mean_imputed.mean(), 15), 
                 xytext=(45, 20), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', color='red'))

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

print("\n⚠️  WHY variance reduction matters:")
print("  - Model thinks ages are more similar than they are")
print("  - Underestimates uncertainty")
print("  - Can hurt performance on regression tasks")
```

**WHEN TO USE:**
- ✅ Few missing values (<10%)
- ✅ Quick baseline
- ✅ Median for outlier-prone data
- ❌ High percentage missing (>20%)
- ❌ When variance matters

### **2B. Mode Imputation (Categorical)**

**WHY:** Most common category is "safest" guess

**Code:**
```python
# Categorical data
colors = ['Red', 'Blue', np.nan, 'Red', np.nan, 'Green', 'Red', 'Blue']

imputer_mode = SimpleImputer(strategy='most_frequent')
colors_imputed = imputer_mode.fit_transform(np.array(colors).reshape(-1, 1))

print("✅ Mode imputation for categorical:")
print(f"  Original: {colors}")
print(f"  Imputed:  {[c[0] for c in colors_imputed]}")
print(f"  Mode: {imputer_mode.statistics_[0]}")
print("\nWHY mode: Most common = most likely if we had to guess")
```

sections.title: Strategy 3: Advanced Imputation
sections.body:
### **3A. K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) Imputation**

**WHY IT'S SMART:**
- Uses **similar samples** to impute
- Captures relationships between features
- More accurate than mean

**WHY IT'S SLOW:**
- Computes distances to all samples
- O(n²) complexity

**Code:**
```python
from sklearn.impute import KNNImputer

# Multi-feature dataset
data = pd.DataFrame({
    'age': [25, 30, np.nan, 45, 50, 28, 60],
    'income': [30000, 45000, 45000, np.nan, 70000, 32000, np.nan],
    'years_employed': [2, 5, 6, np.nan, 20, 3, 25]
})

print("Original data with missing:")
print(data)

# Mean imputation (baseline)
imputer_mean = SimpleImputer(strategy='mean')
data_mean = pd.DataFrame(
    imputer_mean.fit_transform(data),
    columns=data.columns
)

# KNN imputation
imputer_knn = KNNImputer(n_neighbors=3)
data_knn = pd.DataFrame(
    imputer_knn.fit_transform(data),
    columns=data.columns
)

print("\n\nMean imputation:")
print(data_mean)

print("\n✅ KNN imputation:")
print(data_knn)

print("\n\nWHY KNN is better:")
print("  Row 2 (age missing):")
print(f"    Mean imputed age: {data_mean.iloc[2]['age']:.0f}")
print(f"    KNN imputed age:  {data_knn.iloc[2]['age']:.0f}")
print("    → KNN uses similar income/years_employed to estimate age!")

print("\n  Row 3 (income missing):")
print(f"    Mean imputed income: ${data_mean.iloc[3]['income']:.0f}")
print(f"    KNN imputed income:  ${data_knn.iloc[3]['income']:.0f}")
print("    → KNN uses age=45 to find similar people's incomes!")
```

**WHEN TO USE:**
- ✅ Features are correlated
- ✅ MAR (missing depends on other features)
- ✅ Medium datasets (<10k samples)
- ❌ Large datasets (too slow)
- ❌ High-dimensional data

### **3B. Iterative Imputation (MICE)**

**WHY IT'S POWERFUL:**
- Models each feature with missing values using ALL other features
- Iterates until convergence
- **Captures complex relationships**

**WHY IT'S COMPLEX:**
- Slow (multiple iterations)
- Can overfit
- Sensitive to initialization

**Code:**
```python
from sklearn.experimental import enable_iterative_imputer
from sklearn.impute import IterativeImputer

# Complex relationships
data_complex = pd.DataFrame({
    'height_cm': [170, 180, np.nan, 190, 175, np.nan],
    'weight_kg': [65, 80, 95, np.nan, 70, 60],
    'age': [25, 35, 45, 55, 30, np.nan]
})
# Height & weight correlated, age independent

print("Original:")
print(data_complex)

# Iterative imputation
imputer_iter = IterativeImputer(random_state=42, max_iter=10)
data_iter = pd.DataFrame(
    imputer_iter.fit_transform(data_complex),
    columns=data_complex.columns
)

print("\n✅ Iterative imputation:")
print(data_iter)

print("\n\nWHY iterative is smart:")
print("  1. Models height using weight & age")
print("  2. Models weight using height & age")
print("  3. Models age using height & weight")
print("  4. Iterates until stable")
print("  → Captures height-weight correlation!")
```

**WHEN TO USE:**
- ✅ Complex feature relationships
- ✅ MAR (missing depends on others)
- ✅ When accuracy is critical
- ❌ Simple relationships (overkill)
- ❌ Very large datasets

sections.title: Strategy 4: Add Missing Indicator
sections.body:
**WHY THIS IS CLEVER:**
- **Missingness itself might be informative!**
- Let model learn if missing = pattern

**Code:**
```python
from sklearn.impute import MissingIndicator

# Example: Income missing for high earners
data_indicator = pd.DataFrame({
    'age': [25, 30, 35, 45, 50, 60],
    'income': [30000, 45000, np.nan, np.nan, 70000, np.nan]
})

# Add missing indicator
indicator = MissingIndicator()
missing_mask = indicator.fit_transform(data_indicator)

data_indicator['income_missing'] = missing_mask[:, 1]  # Column for income

# Impute
imputer = SimpleImputer(strategy='median')
data_indicator['income_imputed'] = imputer.fit_transform(
    data_indicator[['income']]
)

print("✅ With missing indicator:")
print(data_indicator)

print("\n\nWHY adding indicator helps:")
print("  Model can learn: income_missing=1 → likely high earner!")
print("  Captures MNAR pattern")
print("  Example: If high earners don't report income,")
print("           indicator tells model 'this person is probably rich'")
```

**WHEN TO USE:**
- ✅ MNAR (missing has meaning)
- ✅ Missingness is predictive
- ✅ Always safe to add (worst case: model ignores it)
- ❌ MCAR (no pattern, just noise)

sections.title: Comparison Table
sections.body:
| Method | Speed | Accuracy | Use Case | Bias Risk |
|--------|-------|----------|----------|-----------|
| **Deletion** | ⚡⚡⚡ | Fair | MCAR, <5% missing, large dataset | Low if MCAR |
| **Mean/Median** | ⚡⚡⚡ | Fair | Quick baseline, <10% missing | Reduces variance |
| **Mode** | ⚡⚡⚡ | Fair | Categorical, quick baseline | Can amplify majority class |
| **KNN** | ⚡ | Good | MAR, correlated features | Low |
| **Iterative (MICE)** | ⚡ | Best | Complex relationships, MAR | Can overfit |
| **Add Indicator** | ⚡⚡⚡ | Good | MNAR, always safe | Low |

sections.title: Decision Flowchart
sections.body:
```
How much data is missing?
│
├─ <5% + MCAR → Deletion ✅
│
├─ 5-20% → What's the pattern?
│   │
│   ├─ MCAR → Mean/Median Imputation
│   │
│   ├─ MAR (depends on other features)
│   │   ├─ Simple relationships → KNN Imputation
│   │   └─ Complex relationships → Iterative Imputation
│   │
│   └─ MNAR (missing has meaning)
│       └─ Add Missing Indicator + Impute
│
└─ >20% → Investigate!
     ├─ Drop feature if uninformative
     ├─ Collect more data
     └─ Use advanced techniques (MICE + indicator)
```

sections.title: Common Pitfalls
sections.body:
### **1. Imputing Before Train/Test Split (LEAKAGE!)**
```python
# ❌ WRONG: Test data leaks into training
imputer = SimpleImputer(strategy='mean')
X_all_imputed = imputer.fit_transform(X)  # Uses test set mean!
X_train, X_test = train_test_split(X_all_imputed)

# ✅ CORRECT: Fit on train, transform test
X_train, X_test = train_test_split(X)
imputer = SimpleImputer(strategy='mean')
X_train_imputed = imputer.fit_transform(X_train)  # Train mean only
X_test_imputed = imputer.transform(X_test)         # Use train mean
```

### **2. Not Investigating WHY Data is Missing**
```python
# Always check missing pattern!
print("Missing value analysis:")
print(df.isnull().sum())
print("\nMissing by age group:")
print(df.groupby(pd.cut(df['age'], bins=3))['income'].apply(
    lambda x: x.isnull().sum()
))
# If pattern → MAR or MNAR, need smart imputation!
```

### **3. Using Mean for Skewed Data**
```python
# Income is skewed → use median!
income = [20000, 25000, 30000, 35000, 500000]  # One outlier
print(f"Mean:   ${np.mean(income):,.0f} ← Distorted by outlier!")
print(f"Median: ${np.median(income):,.0f} ← Robust!")
```

sections.title: � Production Pipeline with Imputation
sections.body:
```python
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer, KNNImputer
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
import joblib

# Sample data with missing values
X = pd.DataFrame({
    'age': [25, np.nan, 35, 28, np.nan],
    'income': [50000, 60000, np.nan, 45000, 70000],
    'credit_score': [650, np.nan, 720, 680, np.nan]
})
y = np.array([0, 1, 1, 0, 1])

# Different imputation for different columns
preprocessor = ColumnTransformer([
    ('median_impute', SimpleImputer(strategy='median'), ['age', 'income']),
    ('knn_impute', KNNImputer(n_neighbors=3), ['credit_score'])
])

# Complete pipeline
pipeline = Pipeline([
    ('imputer', preprocessor),
    ('classifier', RandomForestClassifier(random_state=42))
])

# Fit and save
pipeline.fit(X, y)
joblib.dump(pipeline, 'imputation_pipeline.pkl')

# Load and predict (imputation automatic!)
new_data = pd.DataFrame({
    'age': [30],
    'income': [np.nan],  # Missing value!
    'credit_score': [700]
})

loaded_pipeline = joblib.load('imputation_pipeline.pkl')
prediction = loaded_pipeline.predict(new_data)
print(f"✅ Prediction with missing value: {prediction[0]}")
```

sections.title: � Summary
sections.body:
**WHY Handling Missing Values Matters:**
- Most algorithms crash on NaN
- **HOW you impute affects model performance**
- Wrong strategy introduces bias

**Key Insights:**
- **MCAR** (random) → Deletion OK
- **MAR** (depends on others) → KNN/Iterative imputation
- **MNAR** (meaningful missing) → Add indicator!
- Always **add missing indicator** when in doubt

**Best Practices:**
- ✅ Investigate missing pattern first
- ✅ Impute AFTER train/test split
- ✅ Use median for skewed data
- ✅ Add missing indicator for MNAR
- ✅ Compare multiple imputation methods

**Golden Rule:** Missingness can be informative - don't throw away that signal!
